title: 02 · The function checklist
summary: The 58 functions of the course, grouped in the order an analysis uses them, with what each does and one typical call.
question: Which R functions does a whole analysis need, and in what order are they used?

chain.title: How to use the checklist
chain.statement: The sheet lists 58 functions in nine groups that follow an analysis from setting up to programming; tick what you can use without looking it up and circle what to practise.

explain.text: Tags say where each function appears in the course: CP computational practice, P practical, L lecture, and a star for a bonus function not yet in the course files. The groups run in the order of real work: set up, import, inspect, build and pick, summarise, plot, probability, test and model, program.

figure.caption: The nine groups, in the order of an analysis.

terms.meaning: computational practice / practical / lecture / bonus, where the function is taught

chain.intuition: The checklist is the route of an analysis, from opening the folder to writing your own tools.
chain.misconception: Learning functions alphabetically is efficient. Learning them by purpose shows when to use each.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Functions grouped by the step of the analysis they serve.

check.q: Into which group does str() go, and why there?
check.a: Inspect (group 3): you look at the types of the columns before testing anything.

chain.opens: What do you set up once per project before any analysis?
chain.answers: Which R functions does a whole analysis need, and in what order are they used?

chain.title: Set up once per project
chain.statement: getwd() shows the folder R is in, setwd() changes it, install.packages() downloads a package once, library() loads it in every session.

explain.text: A package is downloaded to your computer only once with install.packages(), but it must be loaded with library() in every new R session before its functions exist. The working directory decides where read.csv() looks for files, so check it with getwd() first.

code.interpret: Each line is a typical use; the comment says what comes back.

chain.opens: How do you bring a data file into R?

terms.meaning: a bundle of extra functions; installed once, loaded each session
the folder R reads files from and saves files to

chain.intuition: Installing buys the book; library() takes it off the shelf each day.
chain.misconception: install.packages() is needed every session. Only library() is.

wrong.title: Mistaken
wrong.text: install.packages() every time I open R.

check.q: R says "could not find function viridis". What two causes are likely?
check.a: The package is not installed, or it is installed but not loaded with library().

chain.answers: What do you set up once per project before any analysis?

chain.title: Import
chain.statement: read.csv() reads a comma-separated file into a data frame.

explain.text: read.csv("mammal_sleep_flying.csv") looks for the file in the working directory and returns a data frame: one row per mammal, one column per variable. Store it with dat <- so that later functions can use it.

lines.explain: read the file into a data frame called dat

code.interpret: Each line is a typical use; the comment says what comes back.

chain.opens: What should you look at before you test anything?

terms.meaning: a table: rows are cases, columns are variables

chain.intuition: read.csv() pours the spreadsheet into R as a table.
chain.misconception: read.csv() opens the file wherever it is. It only looks in the working directory unless you give a path.

right.title: Instead
right.text: R looks in getwd() unless you give the full path.

check.q: What does dat <- read.csv("sleep.csv") do if sleep.csv is in another folder?
check.a: It fails with "cannot open file … No such file or directory".

chain.answers: How do you bring a data file into R?

chain.title: Inspect: always look before you test
chain.statement: View(), head(), str(), summary(), dim(), class(), table() and levels() show the data before any test.

explain.text: head(dat) prints the first 6 rows; str(dat) shows every column with its type; summary(dat) gives quick statistics per column, including the number of NAs; dim(dat) gives rows × columns; class() says what type an object is; table() counts each category; levels() lists a factor's categories; View() opens a spreadsheet view.

lines.explain: min, quartiles, mean, max and the number of NAs
how many mammals in each danger level

code.interpret: Each line is a typical use; the comment says what comes back.

chain.opens: How do you build vectors and pick parts of the data?

terms.meaning: a categorical variable with a fixed set of levels

chain.intuition: Look at the patient before you operate.
chain.misconception: If R imported the file without an error, the columns are fine. A numeric column can arrive as text; str() reveals it.

right.title: Instead
right.text: str() first: a number column may be chr.

check.q: Which function tells you how many NAs TotalSleep has?

figure.caption: Values present and missing in TotalSleep.

chain.answers: What should you look at before you test anything?

chain.title: Build & pick
chain.statement: c(), seq() and rep() build vectors; dat[row, col] and dat$col pick parts; length(), as.factor(), as.numeric(), is.na() and which.max() describe and convert them.

explain.text: c(12, 15, 9) combines values into a vector. dat[2, 3] picks row 2, column 3; dat$TotalSleep picks a column by name. length() counts values; as.factor() treats numbers as categories (danger 1–5); as.numeric() converts text to numbers; is.na() marks missing values; which.max() gives the position of the largest value.

lines.explain: the row of the longest sleeper

code.interpret: Each line is a typical use; the comment says what comes back.

terms.meaning: an ordered set of values of one type
pick by position; leave a side empty for all rows or all columns

chain.intuition: Rows are animals, columns are measurements: [row, col] is a grid reference.
chain.misconception: dat[3] is row 3. For a data frame dat[3] is column 3; use dat[3, ] for the row.

right.title: Instead
right.text: dat[3] = third column; dat[3, ] = third row.

check.q: How do you get the TotalSleep of row 10?

chain.answers: How do you build vectors and pick parts of the data?

chain.title: Summarise
chain.statement: mean(), median(), sd(), min(), max(), sum(), IQR(), log() and log10() summarise a column.

explain.text: mean() and median() give the centre (watch the NAs: na.rm = TRUE); sd() and IQR() give the spread, IQR being the range of the middle 50%; min() and max() the extremes; sum() adds up, and on a logical vector it counts the TRUEs; log() and log10() tame skewed data such as body mass.

lines.explain: counts mammals sleeping more than 12 h (TRUE counts as 1)
body mass on a log scale

code.interpret: Each line is a typical use; the comment says what comes back.

chain.opens: How do you see the data as a picture?

terms.meaning: interquartile range: third quartile minus first quartile

chain.intuition: Centre, spread and extremes are the three questions every summary answers.

intuitionFigure.caption: Centre, spread and extremes on one axis (sleep, hours).

chain.misconception: sum() only adds numbers. On TRUE/FALSE values it counts the TRUEs, which makes it a counter.

right.title: Instead
right.text: sum(x > 12) counts how many are above 12.

check.q: Why might the median be better than the mean for body mass?
check.a: Body mass is very skewed (0.005 to 6,654 kg): a few giants drag the mean up; the median is not moved by them.

right.title: Instead
right.text: median = the typical mammal; the mean follows the elephants.

chain.title: Plot (see sheet 04)
chain.statement: plot(), hist(), boxplot(), barplot(), points(), lines(), abline(), legend() and par() draw and annotate graphs.

explain.text: plot(x, y) draws a scatterplot of y against x; hist() a histogram; boxplot(y ~ group) one box per group; barplot() bars. points(), lines() and abline() add dots, lines and a straight line to an existing plot; legend() adds the key of colours and symbols; par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) puts several plots side by side.

lines.explain: add a dashed horizontal line at 10.5 h

code.interpret: Each line is a typical use; the comment says what comes back.

terms.meaning: formula: y as a function of x (response ~ explanatory)

chain.intuition: plot() builds the canvas; points(), lines() and abline() draw on it.
chain.misconception: abline() makes a new plot. It adds to the current one.

right.title: Instead
right.text: abline() adds a line to the open graph.

check.q: Which call draws one box per group?

chain.answers: How do you see the data as a picture?

chain.title: Probability (see sheet 05)
chain.statement: dbinom(), pbinom(), rbinom(), dpois(), dnorm(), pnorm(), qnorm() and rnorm() compute probabilities, quantiles and random values.

explain.text: The first letter says the question: d = density or P(exactly x), p = probability of x or less, q = the value that cuts off a probability, r = random values. The rest of the name is the distribution: binom, pois, norm. Sheet 05 works through each with the natural-killer-cell example.

code.interpret: Each line is a typical use; the comment says what comes back.

chain.opens: Which functions test hypotheses and fit models?
chain.intuition: Four questions, one family of functions per distribution.
chain.misconception: dnorm() gives a probability. For a continuous variable it gives the height of the curve; probabilities are areas (pnorm).

check.q: Which function gives P(X ≤ 3) for a binomial?

chain.title: Test & model (see sheet 06)
chain.statement: shapiro.test(), t.test(), wilcox.test(), chisq.test(), lm(), summary(fit) and cor() test hypotheses and fit models.

explain.text: shapiro.test() asks whether data are close to normal; t.test() compares means; wilcox.test() is its rank-based version for weak or non-normal data; chisq.test() compares counts with expected counts; lm() fits a straight line y = mx + c and summary(fit) reports the slope, intercept and p-values; cor() gives the correlation r.

code.interpret: Each line is a typical use; the comment says what comes back.

chain.opens: How do you write your own repeated steps?

terms.meaning: linear model: fits y = intercept + slope × x by least squares

chain.intuition: Sheet 06 is the map from your data to the right one of these.
chain.misconception: A significant shapiro.test() is good news. A small p means the data are NOT normal.

right.title: Instead
right.text: p > 0.05 → normal enough; p < 0.05 → not normal.

check.q: Which function compares counts with an expected 3:1 ratio?

chain.answers: Which functions test hypotheses and fit models?

chain.title: Program
chain.statement: function(x) { } writes your own function, for (i in 1:n) repeats a step, if () { } else chooses a branch, sapply() applies a function to each element, ?name opens help.

explain.text: A for loop runs its body once for each value of i; if () { } else { } runs one of two branches depending on a TRUE/FALSE condition; sapply(x, f) applies f to every element of x and collects the results, often replacing a loop.

lines.explain: the same squares as a vector: 1 4 9

code.interpret: Each line is a typical use; the comment says what comes back.

chain.opens: How many of the 58 can you use without looking them up?

terms.meaning: repeat a step for each value
apply a function to each element and simplify the result to a vector

chain.intuition: A loop is a conveyor: the same machine handles each item in turn.
chain.misconception: Loops are always needed to repeat work in R.
chain.answers: How do you write your own repeated steps?

chain.title: Your score out of 58
chain.statement: Counting the ticks gives a score out of 58; the circled functions are your practice list for the next session.

explain.text: The score is a self-test, not a grade: retrieval practice (trying to recall before looking) is one of the most effective ways to learn. Re-take the checklist after each practical and watch the circled set shrink.

terms.meaning: learning by recalling from memory rather than re-reading

chain.intuition: The score is a map of what to practise next.

intuitionFigure.caption: Ticks and circles across the nine groups (your own counts go here).

chain.misconception: A low score means you are behind. It means you have a precise practice list.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Low score = a short, precise list to practise.

check.q: Why tick before looking things up?
check.a: Recalling first is the practice; looking up first only tests recognition.
